lesson.title: Relative Abundance: How Much of Each Isotope Actually Exists
lesson.summary: Relative abundance is the percentage of a specific isotope found in a natural sample of an element, measured by mass spectrometry and used to calculate average atomic mass.
lesson.body:
Isotopes explain why an element can have atoms of different masses, but on its own that fact does not say how common each isotope actually is in nature. Relative abundance fills that gap: it is the percentage, or equivalently the fraction, of a naturally occurring sample of an element made up by one particular isotope. Relative abundances for all of an element's isotopes always add up to 100 percent, since every atom in a natural sample must be one isotope or another, no more, no less. Some isotopes dominate a natural sample overwhelmingly, while others exist only in trace amounts.

Relative abundance is measured experimentally using mass spectrometry, which separates a sample's ions by mass-to-charge ratio and records how many ions of each mass arrive at the detector. The height, or more precisely the area, of each peak on the resulting mass spectrum is directly proportional to that isotope's relative abundance, which is why reading peak heights carefully during mass spectrum analysis is the practical method for extracting these percentages from real data. A tall, dominant peak signals a common isotope, while a short peak signals a rare one.

Relative abundance values vary enormously across the periodic table and even across isotopes of the same element. Carbon, for example, is about 98.93 percent carbon-12 and only about 1.07 percent carbon-13 in any natural sample, meaning carbon-12 vastly dominates. Chlorine splits far less unevenly: about 75.76 percent chlorine-35 and 24.24 percent chlorine-37, meaning roughly three chlorine-35 atoms exist for every one chlorine-37 atom in any natural sample of chlorine, whether it is chlorine gas, table salt, or hydrochloric acid.

A worked example shows how relative abundance is used quantitatively. Boron exists as two isotopes: boron-10 with a relative abundance of 19.9 percent, and boron-11 with a relative abundance of 80.1 percent. If you had a hypothetical sample of exactly 1,000 boron atoms drawn from nature, you would expect about 199 of them to be boron-10, since 19.9 percent of 1,000 is 199, and about 801 of them to be boron-11, since 80.1 percent of 1,000 is 801. These two counts add up to the full 1,000 atoms, confirming the abundances account for the entire sample, and this same proportion, converted to decimals, is exactly what gets multiplied by each isotope's atomic mass when calculating average atomic mass.

Relative abundance is not a fixed law of physics in the way atomic number is. It is an empirical measurement of how isotopes happen to be distributed in naturally occurring matter on Earth, shaped by the nuclear physics of how those isotopes formed in stars and how stable each one is over geological time. Because relative abundance is measured rather than derived from theory, mass spectrometry remains the essential tool for determining it accurately, and those measured abundances, combined with each isotope's measured atomic mass, are exactly the two ingredients that average atomic mass calculations combine to produce the values seen on the periodic table.
